full_judgment: 30. P.W. 2 during his cross-examination ad- mitted that under the provisions of Customs Act they are empowered to search and arrest any person and with the backing of that law they searched the appellant and seized the gold and other items. The learned Advocate relying on these statements of P.W. 2 submits that as the statement was made after the arrest of the accused appellant the same is barred under section 24 of the Evidence Act and he relied in the case of State Vs. Balshri Das Sutradhar reported in 13 D.L.R. 289 where it has been held that generally speaking a " person in authority " within the meaning of section 24 of the Evidence Act is one who is engaged in apprehension, detention or prosecution of the accused or one who is empowered to examine him. Here in the present case before us, P.W. 2 categorically stated that they have the power to apprehend, detain and prosecute and examine any person under the Customs Act and in this case the appellant was arrested by the Customs officials for smuggling gold inside Bangladesh and they prosecuted him. In such circumstances it is found that as the statement was admittedly made by the appellant while in custody of the Customs officials the same cannot be considered as evidence and it is barred un-der section 24 of the Evidence Act. Furthermore from the evidence of P.W. 5 it is found that he saw the appellant writing the statement at the dictation of the Customs official. Admittedly the statement was written by the appellant while he was in detention and from the evidence of P.W. 5 it is found that the statement was dictated by the Customs officer and written by the appellant and in such circumstances it cannot be found that the statement was voluntary and may have been secured by some sorts of inducement. When such a statement is secured by some sorts of inducement by the person in authority such confession or statement cannot be considered as evidence and the same is also barred under section 24 of the Evidence Act. This view gets support in the case of Kalipada Nandi Vs. The State reported in A.I.R. 1950 (Cal) page 427 and also in the case of Emperior Vs. Kutub Bux reported in A.I.R. 1930 Cal. 633 relevant page 634. As the statement Ext. 2 was written by the appellant while in custody the same cannot be considered as an evidence and it is barred under section 24 of the Evidence Act. Agreeing with the aforesaid decisions we are of the view that the trial court has committed illegality in placing reliance on this Ext. 2.
